entries.6cf1fb8783837309f93dc17e7a5dd8db4a1c009b: <div sID="gen18524" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Ezek.8" sID="Ezek.8"/> <div eID="gen18524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18525" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18526" type="x-p"/> God, having given the prophet a clear foresight of the people's miseries that were hastening on, here gives him a clear insight into the people's wickedness, by which God was provoked to bring these miseries upon them, that he might justify God in all his judgments, might the more particularly reprove the sins of the people, and with the more satisfaction foretel their ruin. Here God, in vision, brings him to Jerusalem, to show him the sins that were committed there, though God had begun to contend with them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1-Ezek.8.4">ver. 1-4</reference>), and there he sees, I. The image of jealousy set up at the gate of the altar, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.5-Ezek.8.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. II. The elders of Israel worshipping all manner of images in a secret chamber, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.7-Ezek.8.12">ver. 7-12</reference>. III. The women weeping for Tammuz, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.13-Ezek.8.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>. IV. The men worshipping the sun, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.15-Ezek.8.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>. And then appeals to him whether such a provoking people should have any pity shown them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.17-Ezek.8.18">ver. 17, 18</reference>.
entries.e607349c69b5034718caaea096812c1c3aa37589: <div eID="gen18526" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18525" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Divine Glory. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 593.)</title> <div sID="gen18527" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass in the sixth year, in the sixth <hi type="italic">month,</hi> in the fifth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, <hi type="italic">as</hi> I sat in mine house, and the elders of Judah sat before me, that the hand of the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> fell there upon me. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then I beheld, and lo a likeness as the appearance of fire: from the appearance of his loins even downward, fire; and from his loins even upward, as the appearance of brightness, as the colour of amber. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he put forth the form of a hand, and took me by a lock of mine head; and the spirit lifted me up between the earth and the heaven, and brought me in the visions of God to Jerusalem, to the door of the inner gate that looketh toward the north; where <hi type="italic">was</hi> the seat of the image of jealousy, which provoketh to jealousy. <hi type="super">4</hi> And, behold, the glory of the God of Israel <hi type="italic">was</hi> there, according to the vision that I saw in the plain. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then said he unto me, Son of man, lift up thine eyes now the way toward the north. So I lifted up mine eyes the way toward the north, and behold northward at the gate of the altar this image of jealousy in the entry. <hi type="super">6</hi> He said furthermore unto me, Son of man, seest thou what they do? <hi type="italic">even</hi> the great abominations that the house of Israel committeth here, that I should go far off from my sanctuary? but turn thee yet again, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thou shalt see greater abominations. <div eID="gen18527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18528" type="x-p"/> Ezekiel was now in Babylon; but the messages of wrath he had delivered in the foregoing chapters related to Jerusalem, for in the peace or trouble thereof the captives looked upon themselves to have peace or trouble, and therefore here he has a vision of what was done at Jerusalem, and this vision is continued to the close of the 11th chapter. <div eID="gen18528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18529" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the date of this vision. The first vision he had was in <hi type="italic">the fifth year of the captivity, in the fourth month</hi> and <hi type="italic">the fifth day of the month,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.1-Ezek.1.2">ch. i. 1, 2</reference>. This was just fourteen months after. Perhaps it was after he had lain 390 days on his left side, to bear the iniquity of Israel, and before he began the forty days on his right side, to bear the iniquity of Judah; for now he was sitting in the house, not lying. Note, God keeps a particular account of the messages he sends to us, because he will shortly call us to account about them. <div eID="gen18529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18530" type="x-p"/> II. The opportunity is taken notice of, as well as the time. 1. The prophet was himself <hi type="italic">sitting in his house,</hi> in a sedate composed frame, deep perhaps in contemplation. Note, The more we retreat from the world, and retire into our own hearts, the better frame we are in for communion with God: those that sit down to consider what they have learned shall be taught more. Or, he <hi type="italic">sat in his house,</hi> ready to preach to the company that resorted to him, but waiting for instructions what to say. God will communicate more knowledge to those who are communicative of what they do know. 2. <hi type="italic">The elders of Judah,</hi> that were now in captivity with him, <hi type="italic">sat before him.</hi> It is probable that it was on the sabbath day, and that it was usual for them to attend on the prophet every sabbath day, both to hear the word from him and to join with him in prayer and praise: and how could they spend the sabbath better, now that they had neither temple nor synagogue, neither priest nor altar? It was a great mercy that they had opportunity to spend it so well, as the good people in Elisha's time, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.23">2 Kings iv. 23</reference>. But some think it was on some extraordinary occasion that they attended him, to enquire of the Lord, and <hi type="italic">sat down</hi> at his feet to <hi type="italic">hear his word.</hi> Observe here, (1.) When the <hi type="italic">law had perished from the priests</hi> at Jerusalem, whose <hi type="italic">lips should keep knowledge</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.26">ch. vii. 26</reference>), those in Babylon had a prophet to consult. God is not tied to places or persons. (2.) Now that the elders of Judah were in captivity they paid more respect to God's prophets, and his word in their mouth, than they did when they lived in peace in their own land. When God brings men into the <hi type="italic">cords of affliction,</hi> then he <hi type="italic">opens their ears to discipline,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.36.8 Job.36.10">Job xxxvi. 8, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.141.6">Ps. cxli. 6</reference>. Those that despised a vision in the <hi type="italic">valley of vision</hi> prized it now that the word of the Lord was precious and there was <hi type="italic">no open vision.</hi> (3.) When our teachers are driven into corners, and are forced to preach in private houses, we must diligently attend them there. A minister's house should be a church for all his neighbours. Paul preached in his own hired house at Rome, and God owned him there, and <hi type="italic">no man forbad him.</hi> <div eID="gen18530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18531" type="x-p"/> III. The divine influence and impression that the prophet was now under: <hi type="italic">The hand of the Lord fell there upon me.</hi> God's hand took hold of him, and arrested him, as it were, to employ him in this vision, but at the same time supported him to bear it. <div eID="gen18531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18532" type="x-p"/> IV. The vision that the prophet saw, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.2">v. 2</reference>. He <hi type="italic">beheld a likeness,</hi> of a man we may suppose, for that was the likeness he saw before, but it was all <hi type="italic">brightness</hi> above the girdle and all <hi type="italic">fire</hi> below, fire and flame. This agrees with the description we had before of the apparition he saw, <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.27">ch. i. 27</reference>. It is probably that it was the same person, the man Christ Jesus. It is probable that the elders that <hi type="italic">sat with him</hi> (as the men that journeyed with Paul) saw a light and were afraid, and this happy sight they gained by attending the prophet in a private meeting, but they had no distinct view of him that spoke to him, <reference osisRef="Acts.22.9">Acts xxii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen18532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18533" type="x-p"/> V. The prophet's remove, in vision, to Jerusalem. The apparition he saw <hi type="italic">put forth the form of a hand,</hi> which <hi type="italic">took him by a lock of his head,</hi> and the Spirit was that hand which was put forth, for the Spirit of God is called <hi type="italic">the finger of God.</hi> Or, The spirit within him <hi type="italic">lifted him up,</hi> so that he was borne up and carried on by an internal principle, not an external violence. A faithful ready servant of God will be drawn by a hair, by the least intimation of the divine will, to his duty; for he has that within him which inclines him to a compliance with it, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.8">Ps. xxvii. 8</reference>. He was miraculously <hi type="italic">lifted up between heaven and earth,</hi> as if he were to fly away upon eagles' wings. This, it is probable (so Grotius thinks), the elders that sat with him saw; they were witnesses of <hi type="italic">the hand taking him by the lock</hi> of hair, and <hi type="italic">lifting him up,</hi> and then perhaps laying him down again in a trance of ecstasy, while he had the following visions, <hi type="italic">whether in the body or out of the body,</hi> we may suppose, he <hi type="italic">could not tell,</hi> any more than Paul in a like case, much less can we. Note, Those are best prepared for communion with God and the communications of divine light that by divine grace are raised up above the earth and the things of it, to be out of their attractive force. But, being lifted up towards heaven, he was carried in vision to Jerusalem, and to God's sanctuary there; for those that would go to heaven must take that in their way. The Spirit represented to his mind the city and temple as plainly as if he had been there in person. O that by faith we could thus enter into the Jerusalem, the holy city, above, and see the things that are invisible! <div eID="gen18533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18534" type="x-p"/> VI. The discoveries that were made to him there. <div eID="gen18534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18535" type="x-p"/> 1. There he saw the glory of God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, the glory of the God of Israel was there,</hi> the same appearance of the living creatures, and the wheels, and the throne, that he had seen, <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.1-Ezek.1.28">ch. i.</reference> Note, God's servants, wherever they are and whithersoever they go, ought to carry about with them a believing regard to the glory of God and to set that always before them; and those that have seen God's power and glory in the sanctuary should desire to see them again, so as they have seen them, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.2">Ps. lxiii. 2</reference>. Ezekiel has this repeated vision of the glory of God both to give credit to and to put honour upon the following discoveries. But it seems to have a further intention here; it was to aggravate this sin of Israel, in changing their own God, the God of Israel (who is a God of so much glory as here he appears to be), for dunghill gods, scandalous gods, false gods, are indeed no gods. Note, The more glorious we see God to be the more odious we shall see sin to be, especially idolatry, which turns his truth in to a lie, his glory into shame. It was also to aggravate their approaching misery, when this glory of the Lord should remove from them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.23">ch. xi. 23</reference>) and leave the house and city desolate. <div eID="gen18535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18536" type="x-p"/> 2. There he saw the reproach of Israel—and that was <hi type="italic">the image of jealousy,</hi> set <hi type="italic">northward, at the gate of the altar,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.3">v. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.5">5</reference>. What image this was is uncertain, probably an image of Baal, or of the grove, which Manasseh made and set in the temple (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.7">2 Kings xxi. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.3">2 Chron. xxxiii. 3</reference>), which Josiah removed, but his successors, it seems, replaced it there, as probably they did the <hi type="italic">chariots of the sun</hi> which he found <hi type="italic">at the entering in of the house of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">2 Kings xxiii. 11</reference>), and this is here said to be <hi type="italic">in the entry.</hi> But the prophet, instead of telling us what image it was, which might gratify our curiosity, tells us that it was <hi type="italic">the image of jealousy,</hi> to convince our consciences that, whatever image it was, it was in the highest degree offensive to God and <hi type="italic">provoked him to jealousy.</hi> He resented it as a husband would resent the whoredoms of his wife, and would certainly revenge it; for <hi type="italic">God is jealous, and the Lord revenges,</hi> <reference osisRef="Nah.1.2">Nah. i. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen18536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18537" type="x-p"/> (1.) The very setting up of this image <hi type="italic">in the house of the Lord</hi> was enough to <hi type="italic">provoke him to jealousy;</hi> for it is in the matters of his worship that we are particularly told, <hi type="italic">I the Lord thy God am a jealous God.</hi> Those that placed this image at <hi type="italic">the door of the inner gate,</hi> where the people assembled, called <hi type="italic">the gate of the altar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.5">v. 5</reference>), thereby plainly intended, [1.] To affront God, to provoke him to his face, by advancing an idol to be a rival with him for the adoration of his people, in contempt of his law and in defiance of his justice. [2.] To debauch the people, and pick them up as they were entering into the courts of the Lord's house to bring their offerings to him, and to tempt them to offer them to this image; like the adulteress Solomon describes, that <hi type="italic">sits at the door of her house, to call passengers who go right on their ways, Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.9.14-Prov.9.16">Prov. ix. 14-16</reference>. With good reason therefore is this called <hi type="italic">the image of jealousy.</hi> <div eID="gen18537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18538" type="x-p"/> (2.) We may well imagine what a surprise and what a grief it was to Ezekiel to see this image in the house of God, when he was in hopes that the judgments they were under had, by this time, wrought some reformation among them; but there is more wickedness in the world, in the church, than good men think there is. And now, [1.] God appeals to him whether this was not bad enough, and a sufficient ground for God to go upon in casting off this people and abandoning them to ruin. Could he, or any one else, expect any other than <hi type="italic">that God should go far from his sanctuary,</hi> when there were such abominations committed there, in that very place; nay, was he not perfectly driven thence? They did these things designedly, and on purpose that he should leave his sanctuary, and so shall their doom be; they have hereby, in effect, like the Gadarenes, desired him <hi type="italic">to depart out of their coasts,</hi> and therefore he will depart; he will no more dignify and protect his sanctuary, as he has done, but will give it up to reproach and ruin. But, [2.] Though this is bad enough, and serves abundantly to justify God in all that he brings upon them, yet the matter will appear to be much worse: <hi type="italic">But turn thyself yet again,</hi> and thou wilt be amazed to <hi type="italic">see greater abominations than these.</hi> Where there is one abomination it will be found that there are many more. Sins do not go alone.
entries.763e3323bb38472f256f2e0c4417e199868b4a58: <div eID="gen18538" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Secret Abominations Discovered; The Chambers of Imagery. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 593.)</title> <div sID="gen18539" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And he brought me to the door of the court; and when I looked, behold a hole in the wall. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then said he unto me, Son of man, dig now in the wall: and when I had digged in the wall, behold a door. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he said unto me, Go in, and behold the wicked abominations that they do here. <hi type="super">10</hi> So I went in and saw; and behold every form of creeping things, and abominable beasts, and all the idols of the house of Israel, portrayed upon the wall round about. <hi type="super">11</hi> And there stood before them seventy men of the ancients of the house of Israel, and in the midst of them stood Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan, with every man his censer in his hand; and a thick cloud of incense went up. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then said he unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> seeth us not; the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath forsaken the earth. <div eID="gen18539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18540" type="x-p"/> We have here a further discovery of the abominations that were committed at Jerusalem, and within the confines of the temple, too. Now observe, <div eID="gen18540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18541" type="x-p"/> I. How this discovery is made. God, in vision, brought Ezekiel to the <hi type="italic">door of the court,</hi> the outer court, along the sides of which the priests' lodgings were. God could have introduced him at first into <hi type="italic">the chambers of imagery,</hi> but he brings him to them by degrees, partly to employ his own industry in searching out these mysteries of iniquity, and partly to make him sensible with what care and caution those idolaters concealed their idolatries. Before the priests' apartments they had run up a wall, to make them the more private, that they might not lie open to the observation of those who passed by—a shrewd sign that they did something which they had reason to be ashamed of. <hi type="italic">He that doth evil hates the light.</hi> They were not willing that those who saw them in God's house should see them in their own, lest they should see them contradict themselves and undo in private what they did in public. But, <hi type="italic">behold, a hole in the wall,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.7">v. 7</reference>), a spy-hole, by which you might see that which would give cause to suspect them. When hypocrites screen themselves behind the wall of an external profession, and with it think to conceal their wickedness from the eye of the world and carry on their designs the more successfully, it is hard for them to manage it with so much art by that there is some hole or other left in the wall, something that betrays them, to those who look diligently, not to be what they pretend to be. The ass's ears in the fable appeared from under the lion's skin. This <hi type="italic">hole in the wall</hi> Ezekiel made wider, and <hi type="italic">behold a door,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.8">v. 8</reference>. This door he goes in by into <hi type="italic">the treasury,</hi> or some of the apartments of the priests, and sees <hi type="italic">the wicked abominations that they do there,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.9">v. 9</reference>. Note, Those that would discover the mystery of iniquity in others, or in themselves, must accomplish a diligent search; for Satan has his wiles, and depths, and devices, which we should not be ignorant of, and <hi type="italic">the heart is deceitful above all things;</hi> in the examining of it therefore we are concerned to be very strict. <div eID="gen18541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18542" type="x-p"/> II. What the discovery is. It is a very melancholy one. 1. He sees a chamber set round with idolatrous pictures (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">All the idols of the house of Israel,</hi> which they had borrowed from the neighbouring nations, were <hi type="italic">portrayed upon the wall round about,</hi> even the vilest of them, <hi type="italic">the forms of creeping things,</hi> which they worshipped, and <hi type="italic">beasts,</hi> even <hi type="italic">abominable ones,</hi> which are poisonous and venomous; at least they were abominable when they were worshipped. This was a sort of pantheon, a collection of all the idols together which they paid their devotions to. Though the second commandment, in the letter of it, forbids only graven images, yet painted ones are as bad and as dangerous. 2. He sees this chamber filled with idolatrous worshippers (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.11">v. 11</reference>): There were <hi type="italic">seventy men of the elders of Israel</hi> offering incense to these painted idols. Here was a great number of idolaters strengthening one another's hands in this wickedness; though it was in a private chamber, and the meeting industriously concealed, yet here were seventy men engaged in it. I doubt these elders were many more than those in Babylon that sat before the prophet in his house, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1">v. 1</reference>. They were <hi type="italic">seventy men,</hi> the number of the great Sanhedrim, or chief council of the nation, and, we have reason to fear, the same men; for they were <hi type="italic">the ancients of the house of Israel,</hi> not only in age, but in office, who were bound, by the duty of their place, to restrain and punish idolatry and to destroy and abolish all superstitious images wherever they found them; yet these were those that did themselves worship them in private, so undermining that religion which in public they professed to own and promote only because by it they held their preferments. They had <hi type="italic">every man his censer in his hand;</hi> so fond were they of the idolatrous service that they would all be their own priests, and very prodigal they were of their perfumes in honour of these images, for <hi type="italic">a thick cloud of incense went up,</hi> that filled the room. O that the zeal of these idolaters might shame the worshippers of the true God out of their indifference to his service! The prophet took particular notice of one whom he knew, who <hi type="italic">stood in the midst of</hi> these idolaters, as chief among them, being perhaps president of the great council at this time or most forward in this wickedness. No wonder the people were corrupt when the elders were so. The sins of leaders are leading sins. <div eID="gen18542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18543" type="x-p"/> III. What the remark is that made upon it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Son of man, hast thou seen this?</hi> Couldst thou have imagined that there was such wickedness committed?" It is here observed concerning it, 1. That it was done <hi type="italic">in the dark;</hi> for sinful works are <hi type="italic">works of darkness.</hi> They concealed it, lest they should lose their places, or at least their credit. There is a great deal of secret wickedness in the world, which the day will declare, <hi type="italic">the day of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God.</hi> 2. That this one idolatrous chapel was but a specimen of many the like. Here they met together, to worship their images in concert, but, it should seem, they had <hi type="italic">every man the chamber of his imagery</hi> besides, a room in his own house for this purpose, in which every man gratified his own fancy with such pictures as he liked best. Idolaters had their household gods, and their family worship of them in private, which is a shame to those who call themselves Christians and yet have no church in their house, no worship of God in their family. Had they <hi type="italic">chambers of imagery,</hi> and shall not we have chambers of devotion? 3. That atheism was at the bottom of their idolatry. They worship images <hi type="italic">in the dark,</hi> the images of the gods of other nations, and <hi type="italic">they say,</hi> "Jehovah, the God of Israel, whom we should serve, <hi type="italic">seeth us not.</hi> Jehovah <hi type="italic">hath forsaken the earth,</hi> and we may worship what God we will; he regards us not." (1.) They think themselves out of God's sight: <hi type="italic">They say, The Lord seeth us not.</hi> They imagined, because the matter was carried on so closely that men could not discover it, nor did any of their neighbours suspect them to be idolaters, that therefore it was hidden from the eye of God; as if there were any <hi type="italic">darkness, or shadow of death, where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves.</hi> Note, A practical disbelief of God's omniscience is at the bottom of our treacherous departures from him; but the church argues justly, as to this very sin of idolatry (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.20-Ps.44.21">Ps. xliv. 20, 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">If we have forgotten the name of our God, and stretched forth our hand to a strange god, will not God search this out?</hi> No doubt he will. (2.) They think themselves out of God's care: "<hi type="italic">The Lord has forsaken the earth,</hi> and looks not after the affairs of it; and then we may as well worship any other god as him." Or, "He has forsaken our land, and left it to be a prey to its enemies; and therefore it is time for us to look out for some other god, to whom to commit the protection of it. Our one God cannot, or will not, deliver us; and therefore let us have many." This was a blasphemous reflection upon God, as if he had forsaken them first, else they would not have forsaken him. Note, Those are ripe indeed for ruin who have arrived at such a pitch of impudence as to lay the blame of their sins upon God himself.
entries.b3b3b4ff342b7ed84380b5ea95d76331a88bbf0b: <div eID="gen18543" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Chambers of Imagery. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 593.)</title> <div sID="gen18544" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> He said also unto me, Turn thee yet again, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thou shalt see greater abominations that they do. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then he brought me to the door of the gate of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house which <hi type="italic">was</hi> toward the north; and, behold, there sat women weeping for Tammuz. <hi type="super">15</hi> Then said he unto me, Hast thou seen <hi type="italic">this,</hi> O son of man? turn thee yet again, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thou shalt see greater abominations than these. <hi type="super">16</hi> And he brought me into the inner court of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house, and, behold, at the door of the temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , between the porch and the altar, <hi type="italic">were</hi> about five and twenty men, with their backs toward the temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and their faces toward the east; and they worshipped the sun toward the east. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then he said unto me, Hast thou seen <hi type="italic">this,</hi> O son of man? Is it a light thing to the house of Judah that they commit the abominations which they commit here? for they have filled the land with violence, and have returned to provoke me to anger: and, lo, they put the branch to their nose. <hi type="super">18</hi> Therefore will I also deal in fury: mine eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity: and though they cry in mine ears with a loud voice, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> will I not hear them. <div eID="gen18544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18545" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen18545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18546" type="x-p"/> I. More and greater abominations discovered to the prophet. He thought that what he had seen was bad enough and yet (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Turn thyself again, and thou shalt see yet greater abominations,</hi> and greater still, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.15">v. 15</reference>, as before, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.6">v. 6</reference>. There are those who live in retirement who do no think what wickedness there is in this world; and the more we converse with it, and the further we go abroad into it, the more corrupt we see it. When we have seen that which is bad we may have our wonder at it made to cease by the discovery of that which, upon some account or other, is a great deal worse. We shall find it so in examining our own hearts and searching into them; there is a world of iniquity in them, a great abundance and variety of abominations, and, when we have found out much amiss, still we shall find more; for <hi type="italic">the heart is desperately wicked, who can know it</hi> perfectly? Now the abominations here discovered were, 1. <hi type="italic">Women weeping for Tammuz,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.14">v. 14</reference>. An abominable thing indeed, that any should choose rather to serve an idol in tears than to serve the true God <hi type="italic">with joyfulness and gladness of heart!</hi> Yet such absurdities as these are those guilty of who <hi type="italic">follow after lying vanities</hi> and <hi type="italic">forsake their own mercies.</hi> Some think it was for Adonis, an idol among the Greeks, other for Osiris, an idol of the Egyptians, that they shed these tears. The image, they say, was made to weep, and then the worshippers wept with it. They bewailed the death of this Tammuz, and anon rejoiced in its returning to life again. These mourning women <hi type="italic">sat at the door of the gate of the Lord's house,</hi> and there shed their idolatrous tears, as it were in defiance of God and the sacred rites of his worship, and some think, with their idolatry, prostrating themselves also to corporeal whoredom; for these two commonly went together, and those that dishonoured the divine nature by the one were justly <hi type="italic">given up to vile affections</hi> and a reprobate sense to dishonour the human nature, which nowhere ever sunk so far below itself as in these idolatrous rites. 2. <hi type="italic">Men worshipping the sun,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.16">v. 16</reference>. And this was so much the greater an abomination that it was practised <hi type="italic">in the inner court of the Lord's house at the door of the temple of the lord, between the porch and the altar.</hi> There, where the most sacred rites of their holy religion used to be performed, was this abominable wickedness committed. Justly might God in jealousy say to those who thus affronted him at his own door, as the king to Haman, <hi type="italic">Will he force the queen also before me in the house?</hi> Here <hi type="italic">were about twenty-five men</hi> giving that honour to the sun which is due to God only. Some think they were the king and his princes; it should rather seem that they were priests, for this was the court of the priests, and the proper place to find them in. Those that were entrusted with the true religion, had it committed to their care and were charged with the custody of it, they were the men that betrayed it. (1.) They turned <hi type="italic">their backs towards the temple of the Lord,</hi> resolvedly forgetting it and designedly slighting it and putting contempt upon it. Note, When men turn their backs upon God's institutions, and despise them, it is no marvel if they wander endlessly after their own inventions. Impiety is the beginning of idolatry and all iniquity. (2.) They turned <hi type="italic">their faces towards the east, and worshipped the sun,</hi> the rising sun. This was an ancient instance of idolatry; it is mentioned in Job's time (<reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job xxxi. 26</reference>), and had been generally practised among the nations, some worshipping the sun under one name, others under another. These priests, finding it had antiquity and general consent and usage on its side (the two pleas which the papists use at this day in defence of their superstitious rites, and particularly this of worshipping towards the east), practised it in the court of the temple, thinking it an omission that it was not inserted in their ritual. See the folly of idolaters in worshipping that as a god, and calling it <hi type="italic">Baal—a lord,</hi> which God made to be a servant to the universe (for such the sun is, and so his name <hi type="italic">Shemesh</hi> signified, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">Deut. iv. 19</reference>), and in adoring the borrowed light and despising the <hi type="italic">Father of lights.</hi> <div eID="gen18546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18547" type="x-p"/> II. The inference drawn from these discoveries (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hast thou seen this, O son of man!</hi> and couldst thou have thought ever to see such things done in the temple of the Lord?" Now, 1. He appeals to the prophet himself concerning the heinousness of the crime. Can he think it <hi type="italic">is a light thing to the house of Judah,</hi> who know and profess better things, and are dignified with so many privileges above other nations? Is it an excusable thing in those that have God's oracles and ordinances <hi type="italic">that they commit the abominations which they commit here?</hi> Do not those deserve to suffer that thus sin? Should not such abominations as these <hi type="italic">make desolate?</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Dan. ix. 27</reference>. 2. He aggravates it from the fraud and oppression that were to be found in all parts of the nations: <hi type="italic">They have filled the land with violence.</hi> It is not strange if those that wrong God thus make no conscience of wronging one another, and with all that is sacred trample likewise upon all that is just. And their wickedness in their conversations made even the worship they paid to their own God an abomination (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Isa. i. 11</reference>, &c.): "<hi type="italic">They fill the land with violence,</hi> and then they return to the temple <hi type="italic">to provoke me to anger</hi> there; for even their sacrifices, instead of making an atonement, do but add to their guilt. They <hi type="italic">return to provoke me</hi> (they repeat the provocation, do it, and do it again), <hi type="italic">and, lo, they put the branch to their nose</hi>"—a proverbial expression denoting perhaps their scoffing at God and having him in derision; they snuffed at his service, as men do when they <hi type="italic">put a branch to their nose.</hi> Or it was some custom used by idolaters in honour of the idols they served. We read of garlands used in their idolatrous worships (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.13">Acts xiv. 13</reference>), out of which every zealot took a branch which they smelled to as a nosegay. Dr. Lightfoot (<hi type="italic">Hor. Heb. in John</hi> 15.6) gives another sense of this place: <hi type="italic">They put the branch to their wrath,</hi> or <hi type="italic">to his wrath,</hi> as the Masorites read it; that is, they are still bringing more fuel (such as the withered branches of the vine) to the fire of divine wrath, which they have already kindled, as if that wrath did not burn hot enough already. Or putting the branch to the nose may signify the giving of a very great affront and provocation either to God or man; they are an abusive generation of men. 3. He passes sentence upon them that they shall be utterly cut off: <hi type="italic">Therefore,</hi> because they are thus furiously bent upon sin, <hi type="italic">I will also deal in fury</hi> with them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.18">v. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">They filled the land with their violence,</hi> and God will fill it with the violence of their enemies; and he will not lend a favourable ear to the suggestions either, (1.) Of his own pity: <hi type="italic">My eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity;</hi> repentance shall be hidden from his eyes; or, (2.) Of their prayers: <hi type="italic">Though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, yet will I not hear them;</hi> for still their sins cry more loudly for vengeance than their prayers cry for mercy. God will now be as deaf to their prayers as their own idols were, on whom they cried aloud, but in vain, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.26">1 Kings xviii. 26</reference>. Time was when God was ready to hear even <hi type="italic">before they cried</hi> and to <hi type="italic">answer while they were yet speaking;</hi> but now <hi type="italic">they shall seek me early and not find me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.28">Prov. i. 28</reference>. It is not the loud voice, but the upright heart, that God will regard.  <chapter eID="Ezek.8"/> <div eID="gen18547" type="x-p"/>

entries.317470556c924c46251ab69c769c8b924e17ab1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11069"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <div sID="gen19937" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1-Ezek.8.18">Eze 8:1-18</reference>.<div eID="gen19937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19938" type="x-p"/> This eighth chapter begins a new stage of Ezekiel's prophecies and continues to the end of the eleventh chapter. The connected visions at Eze 3:12-7:27 comprehended Judah and Israel; but the visions (Eze 8:<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.25">1-11:25</reference>) refer immediately to Jerusalem and the remnant of Judah under Zedekiah, as distinguished from the Babylonian exiles.<div eID="gen19938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11069"/><hi type="bold">1. sixth year--</hi>namely, of the captivity of Jehoiachin, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.2">Eze 1:2</reference>, the "fifth year" is specified. The lying on his sides three hundred ninety and forty days (<reference osisRef="Ezek.4.5">Eze 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.6">6</reference>) had by this time been completed, at least in vision. That event was naturally a memorable epoch to the exiles; and the computation of years from it was to humble the Jews, as well as to show their perversity in not having repented, though so long and severely chastised.<div eID="gen19939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">elders--</hi>namely, those carried away with Jehoiachin, and now at the Chebar.<div eID="gen19940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sat before me--</hi>to hear the word of God from me, in the absence of the temple and other public places of Sabbath worship, during the exile (<reference osisRef="Ezek.33.30">Eze 33:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.31">31</reference>). It was so ordered that they were present at the giving of the prophecy, and so left without excuse.<div eID="gen19941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hand of ... Lord God fell ... upon me--</hi>God's mighty operation fell, like a thunderbolt, upon me (in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.3">Eze 1:3</reference>, it is less forcible, "was upon him"); whatever, therefore, he is to utter is not his own, for he has put off the mere man, while the power of God reigns in him [Calvin]. <div eID="gen19942" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb3c9d634947e988a32687ee8cf0759869d09717: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11070"/><div sID="gen19943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11070"/><hi type="bold">2. likeness--</hi>understand, "of a man," that is, of Messiah, the Angel of the covenant, in the person of whom alone God manifests Himself (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.26">Eze 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>). The "fire," from "His loins downward," betokens the vengeance of God kindled against the wicked Jews, while searching and purifying the remnant to be spared. The "brightness ... upward" betokens His unapproachable majesty (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:16</reference>). For Hebrew, eesh, "fire," the Septuagint, &c., read ish, "a man."<div eID="gen19943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19944" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">colour of amber--</hi>the glitter of chasmal [Fairbairn], (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.4">Eze 1:4</reference>, "polished brass"). <div eID="gen19944" type="x-p"/>
entries.44f2c746bf01368164cf7bf328abbaec0a8437b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11071"/><div sID="gen19945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11071"/>3. Instead of prompting him to address directly the elders before him, the Spirit carried him away in vision (not in person bodily) to the temple at Jerusalem; he proceeds to report to them what he witnessed: his message thus falls into two parts: (1) The abominations reported in Eze 8:1-18. (2) The dealings of judgment and mercy to be adopted towards the impenitent and penitent Israelites respectively (Eze 9:<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.25">1-11:25</reference>). The exiles looked hopefully towards Jerusalem and, so far from believing things there to be on the verge of ruin, expected a return in peace; while those left in Jerusalem eyed the exiles with contempt, as if cast away from the Lord, whereas they themselves were near God and ensured in the possessions of the land (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.15">Eze 11:15</reference>). Hence the vision here of what affected those in Jerusalem immediately was a seasonable communication to the exiles away from it.<div eID="gen19945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">door of the inner gate--</hi>facing the north, the direction in which he came from Chebar, called the "altar-gate" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.5">Eze 8:5</reference>); it opened into the inner court, wherein stood the altar of burnt offering; the inner court (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.36">1Ki 6:36</reference>) was that of the priests; the outer court (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.5">Eze 10:5</reference>), that of the people, where they assembled.<div eID="gen19946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seat--</hi>the pedestal of the image.<div eID="gen19947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">image of jealousy--</hi>Astarte, or Asheera (as the Hebrew for "grove" ought to be translated, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.3">2Ki 21:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.4">23:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.7">7</reference>), set up by Manasseh as a rival to Jehovah in His temple, and arresting the attention of all worshippers as they entered; it was the Syrian Venus, worshipped with licentious rites; the "queen of heaven," wife of Phoenician Baal. Havernick thinks all the scenes of idolatry in the chapter are successive portions of the festival held in honor of Tammuz or Adonis (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.14">Eze 8:14</reference>). Probably, however, the scenes are separate proofs of Jewish idolatry, rather than restricted to one idol.<div eID="gen19948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">provoketh to jealousy--</hi>calleth for a visitation in wrath of the "jealous God," who will not give His honor to another (compare the second commandment, <reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Ex 20:5</reference>). Jerome refers this verse to a statue of Baal, which Josiah had overthrown and his successors had replaced. <div eID="gen19949" type="x-p"/>
entries.23b2879ac924b3554de59e0c9680731950224ccc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11072"/><div sID="gen19950" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11072"/>4. The Shekinah cloud of Jehovah's glory, notwithstanding the provocation of the idol, still remains in the temple, like that which Ezekiel saw "in the plain" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.22">Eze 3:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.23">23</reference>); not till <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.4">Eze 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.18">18</reference> did it leave the temple at Jerusalem, showing the long-suffering of God, which ought to move the Jews to repentance. <div eID="gen19950" type="x-p"/>
entries.77dfe99772ddefd1cdf4e961dcc8dcfea0856e88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11073"/><div sID="gen19951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11073"/><hi type="bold">5. gate of ... altar--</hi>the principal avenue to the altar of burnt offering; as to the northern position, see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.14">2Ki 16:14</reference>. Ahaz had removed the brazen altar from the front of the Lord's house to the north of the altar which he had himself erected. The locality of the idol before God's own altar enhances the heinousness of the sin. <div eID="gen19951" type="x-p"/>
entries.27ec84a83e54d3d327c00edf868f5799654c04c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11074"/><div sID="gen19952" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11074"/><hi type="bold">6. that I should go far off from my sanctuary--</hi>"that I should (be compelled by their sin to) go far off from my sanctuary"--(<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.18">Eze 10:18</reference>); the sure precursor of its destruction. <div eID="gen19952" type="x-p"/>
entries.42e8f1884fda3b50ce2f8e5458d521198955ff3e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11075"/><div sID="gen19953" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11075"/><hi type="bold">7. door of the court--</hi>that is, of the inner court (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.3">Eze 8:3</reference>); the court of the priests and Levites, into which now others were admitted in violation of the law [Grotius].<div eID="gen19953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hole in ... wall--</hi>that is, an aperture or window in the wall of the priests' chambers, through which he could see into the various apartments, wherein was the idolatrous shrine. <div eID="gen19954" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc9c1063363758e5c30638bb42ae4d788a3a6d76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11076"/><div sID="gen19955" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11076"/><hi type="bold">8. dig--</hi>for it had been blocked up during Josiah's reformation. Or rather, the vision is not of an actual scene, but an ideal pictorial representation of the Egyptian idolatries into which the covenant-people had relapsed, practising them in secret places where they shrank from the light of day [Fairbairn], (<reference osisRef="John.3.20">Joh 3:20</reference>). But compare, as to the literal introduction of idolatries into the temple, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.11">Eze 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.30">Jr 7:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.34">32:34</reference>. <div eID="gen19955" type="x-p"/>
entries.27205aa25412cd4826679070bf3de5e88ce6d9a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11077"/><div sID="gen19956" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11077"/><hi type="bold">10. creeping things ... beasts--</hi>worshipped in Egypt; still found portrayed on their chamber walls; so among the Troglodytæ.<div eID="gen19956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">round about--</hi>On every side they surrounded themselves with incentives to superstition. <div eID="gen19957" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f10c9c8d6080238282b114a9f92cc91a87b1949: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11078"/><div sID="gen19958" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11078"/><hi type="bold">11. seventy men--</hi>the seventy members composing the Sanhedrim, or great council of the nation, the origination of which we find in the seventy elders, representatives of the congregation, who went up with Moses to the mount to behold the glory of Jehovah, and to witness the secret transactions relating to the establishment of the covenant; also, in the seventy elders appointed to share the burden of the people with Moses. How awfully it aggravates the national sin, that the seventy, once admitted to the Lord's secret council (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Psa 25:14</reference>), should now, "in the dark," enter "the secret" of the wicked (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.6">Ge 49:6</reference>), those judicially bound to suppress idolatry being the ringleaders of it!<div eID="gen19958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19959" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jaazaniah--</hi>perhaps chief of the seventy: son of Shaphan, the scribe who read to Josiah the book of the law; the spiritual privileges of the son (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.10-2Kgs.22.14">2Ki 22:10-14</reference>) increased his guilt. The very name means, "Jehovah hears," giving the lie to the unbelief which virtually said (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.9">Eze 9:9</reference>), "The Lord seeth us not," &c. (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">Psa 10:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.21">50:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.7">94:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.9">9</reference>). The offering of incense belonged not to the elders, but to the priests; this usurpation added to the guilt of the former.<div eID="gen19959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19960" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cloud of incense--</hi>They spared no expense for their idols. Oh, that there were the same liberality toward the cause of God! <div eID="gen19960" type="x-p"/>
entries.077406c6a0e2bd9199bea334d21ba233be923fcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11079"/><div sID="gen19961" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11079"/><hi type="bold">12. every man in ... chambers of ... imagery--</hi>The elders ("ancients") are here the representatives of the people, rather than to be regarded literally. Mostly, the leaders of heathen superstitions laughed at them secretly, while publicly professing them in order to keep the people in subjection. Here what is meant is that the people generally addicted themselves to secret idolatry, led on by their elders; there is no doubt, also, allusion to the mysteries, as in the worship of Isis in Egypt, the Eleusinian in Greece, &c., to which the initiated alone were admitted. "The chambers of imagery" are their own perverse imaginations, answering to the priests' chambers in the vision, whereon the pictures were portrayed (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.10">Eze 8:10</reference>).<div eID="gen19961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19962" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord ... forsaken ... earth--</hi>They infer this because God has left them to their miseries, without succoring them, so that they seek help from other gods. Instead of repenting, as they ought, they bite the curb [Calvin]. <div eID="gen19962" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec68484387a6258cabba1034be96d92fff2a1e6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11080"/><div sID="gen19963" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11080"/>14. From the secret abominations of the chambers of imagery, the prophet's eye is turned to the outer court at the north door; within the outer court women were not admitted, but only to the door.<div eID="gen19963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19964" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sat--</hi>the attitude of mourners (<reference osisRef="Job.2.13">Job 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.26">Is 3:26</reference>).<div eID="gen19964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tammuz--</hi>from a Hebrew root, "to melt down." Instead of weeping for the national sins, they wept for the idol. Tammuz (the Syrian for Adonis), the paramour of Venus, and of the same name as the river flowing from Lebanon; killed by a wild boar, and, according to the fable, permitted to spend half the year on earth, and obliged to spend the other half in the lower world. An annual feast was celebrated to him in June (hence called Tammuz in the Jewish calendar) at Byblos, when the Syrian women, in wild grief, tore off their hair and yielded their persons to prostitution, consecrating the hire of their infamy to Venus; next followed days of rejoicing for his return to the earth; the former feast being called "the disappearance of Adonis," the latter, "the finding of Adonis." This Phoenician feast answered to the similar Egyptian one in honor of Osiris. The idea thus fabled was that of the waters of the river and the beauties of spring destroyed by the summer heat. Or else, the earth being clothed with beauty, during the half year when the sun is in the upper hemisphere, and losing it when he departs to the lower. The name Adonis is not here used, as Adon is the appropriated title of Jehovah. <div eID="gen19965" type="x-p"/>
entries.19da22ad1501a95394ec455b4ca8eca11b6522fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11081"/><div sID="gen19966" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11081"/>15-16. The next are "greater abominations," not in respect to the idolatry, but in respect to the place and persons committing it. In "the inner court," immediately before the door of the temple of Jehovah, between the porch and the altar, where the priests advanced only on extraordinary occasions (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.17">Joe 2:17</reference>), twenty-five men (the leaders of the twenty-four courses or orders of the priests, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.18">1Ch 24:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.19">19</reference>, with the high priest, "the princes of the sanctuary," <reference osisRef="Isa.43.28">Is 43:28</reference>), representing the whole priesthood, as the seventy elders represented the people, stood with their backs turned on the temple, and their faces towards the east, making obeisance to the rising sun (contrast <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.44">1Ki 8:44</reference>). Sun-worship came from the Persians, who made the sun the eye of their god Ormuzd. It existed as early as Job (<reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">De 4:19</reference>). Josiah could only suspend it for the time of his reign (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">2Ki 23:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">11</reference>); it revived under his successors. <div eID="gen19966" type="x-p"/>
entries.80314b23332328a77cbf1dc81fbc5db02a103274: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11083"/><div sID="gen19968" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11083"/><hi type="bold">17. put ... branch to ... nose--</hi>proverbial, for "they turn up the nose in scorn," expressing their insolent security [Septuagint]. Not content with outraging "with their violence" the second table of the law, namely, that of duty towards one's neighbor, "they have returned" (that is, they turn back afresh) to provoke Me by violations of the first table [Calvin]. Rather, they held up a branch or bundle of tamarisk (called barsom) to their nose at daybreak, while singing hymns to the rising sun [Strabo, 1.15, p. 733]. Sacred trees were frequent symbols in idol-worship. Calvin translates, "to their own ruin," literally, "to their nose," that is, with the effect of rousing My anger (of which the Hebrew is "nose") to their ruin. <div eID="gen19968" type="x-p"/>
entries.24c11ac54e535ba219050e9c82b2b7e3b8f59ef5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11084"/><div sID="gen19969" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11084"/><hi type="bold">18. though they cry ... yet will I not hear--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.1.28">Pr 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Is 1:15</reference>). <chapter eID="Ezek.8"/>

entries.bfc91e8e74332afbdd68deea220cbc7a68cb8590: <div eID="gen31387" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31388" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31389" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31389" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31388" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31390" type="x-p"/> Here begins a section of prophecy extending to the twelfth chapter. In this chapter the prophet is carried in vision to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Eze.8.1-Eze.8.4">Eze 8:1-4</reference>; and there shown the idolatries committed by the rulers of the Jews, even within the temple. In the beginning of this vision, by the noblest stretch of an inspired imagination, idolatry itself is personified, and made an idol; and the image sublimely called, from the provocation it gave God, the Image of Jealousy, <reference osisRef="Eze.8.5">Eze 8:5</reference>. The prophet then proceeds to describe the three principal superstitions of this unhappy people: the Egyptian, <reference osisRef="Eze.8.6-Eze.8.12">Eze 8:6-12</reference>, the Phoenician, <reference osisRef="Eze.8.13">Eze 8:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.8.14">Eze 8:14</reference>, and the Persian, <reference osisRef="Eze.8.15">Eze 8:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.8.16">Eze 8:16</reference>; giving the striking features of each, and concluding with a declaration of the heinousness of their sins in the sight of God, and the consequent greatness of their punishment, <reference osisRef="Eze.8.17">Eze 8:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.8.18">Eze 8:18</reference>. <div eID="gen31390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31391" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen31391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31392" type="x-p"/> In the sixth year, in the sixth month, in the fifth day of the month - This, according to Abp. Usher, was the sixth year of Ezekiel's captivity. The sixth day of the fifth month of the ecclesiastical year, which answers to August A.M. 3410. <div eID="gen31392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31393" type="x-p"/> This chapter and the three following contain but one vision, of which I judge it necessary, with Calmet, to give a general idea, that the attention of the reader may not be too much divided. <div eID="gen31393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31394" type="x-p"/> The prophet, in the visions of God, is carried to Jerusalem, to the northern gate of the temple, which leads by the north side to the court of the priests. There he sees the glory of the Lord in the same manner as he did by the river Chebar. At one side he sees the image of jealousy. Going thence to the court of the people, he sees through an opening in the wall seventy elders of the people, who were worshipping all sorts of beasts and reptiles, which were painted on the wall. Being brought thence to the gate of the door of the house, he saw women weeping for Tammuz or Adonis. As he returned to the court of the priests, between the porch and the altar, he saw twenty-five men with their backs to the sanctuary and their faces towards the east, worshipping the rising sun. This is the substance of the vision contained in the eighth chapter. <div eID="gen31394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31395" type="x-p"/> About the same time he saw six men come from the higher gate with swords in their hands; and among them, one with an ink-horn. Then the Divine Presence left the cherubim, and took post at the entrance of the temple, and gave orders to the man with the ink-horn to put a mark on the foreheads of those who sighed and prayed because of the abominations of the land; and then commanded the men with the swords to go forward, and slay every person who had not this mark. The prophet, being left alone among the dead, fell on his face, and made intercession for the people. The Lord gives him the reason of his conduct; and the man with the ink-horn returns, and reports to the Lord what was done. These are the general contents of the ninth chapter. <div eID="gen31395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31396" type="x-p"/> The Lord commands the same person to go in between the wheels of the cherubim, and take his hand full of live coals, and scatter them over the city. He went as commanded, and one of the cherubim gave him the coals; at the same time the glory of the Lord, that had removed to the threshold of the house, now returned, and stood over the cherubim. The cherubim, wheels, wings, etc., are here described as in the first chapter. This is the substance of the tenth chapter. <div eID="gen31396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31397" type="x-p"/> The prophet then finds himself transported to the east gate of the temple, where he saw twenty-five men, and among them Jaazaniah the son of Azur, and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people, against whom the Lord commands him to prophesy, and to threaten them with the utmost calamities, because of their crimes. Afterwards God himself speaks, and shows that the Jews who should be left in the land should be driven out because of their iniquities, and that those who had been led captive, and who acknowledged their sins and repented of them, should be restored to their own land. Then the glory of the Lord arose out of the city, and rested for a time on one of the mountains on the east of Jerusalem, and the prophet being carried in vision by the Spirit to Chaldea, lost sight of the chariot of the Divine glory, and began to show to the captivity what the Lord had shown to him. This is the substance of the eleventh chapter. <div eID="gen31397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31398" type="x-p"/> We may see from all this what induced the Lord to abandon his people, his city, and his temple; the abominations of the people in public and in private. But because those carried away captives with Jeconiah acknowledged their sins, and their hearts turned to the Lord, God informs them that they shall be brought back and restored to a happy state both in temporal and spiritual matters, while the others, who had filled up the measure of their iniquities, should be speedily brought into a state of desolation and ruin. This is the sum and intent of the vision in these four chapters.
entries.5bc077fb4d36b4aac010a87310fc3a20d0fb675b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31399" type="x-p"/> The appearance of fire - See the note on <reference osisRef="Eze.1.27">Eze 1:27</reference>.
entries.1cbb8d373d5897cb911e072c937766c7b9c8c3c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen31399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31400" type="x-p"/> The image of jealousy - סמל הקנאה semel hakkinah. We do not know certainly of what form this image was, nor what god it represented. Some say it was the image of Baal, which was placed in the temple by Manasses; others, that it was the image of Mars; and others, that it was the image of Tammuz or Adonis. Calmet supports this opinion by the following reasons: - <div eID="gen31400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31401" type="x-p"/> 1. The name agrees perfectly with him. He was represented as a beautiful youth, beloved by Venus; at which Mars, her paramour, being incensed and filled with jealousy, sent a large boar against Adonis, which killed him with his tusks. Hence it was the image of him who fell a victim to jealousy. <div eID="gen31401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31402" type="x-p"/> 2. The prophet being returned towards the northern gate, where he had seen the image of jealousy, <reference osisRef="Eze.8.14">Eze 8:14</reference>, there saw the women lamenting for Tammuz. Now Tammuz, all agree, signifies Adonis; it was that therefore which was called the image of jealousy. <div eID="gen31402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31403" type="x-p"/> 3. The Scripture often gives to the heathen idols names of degradation; as Baal-zebub, god of flies; Baal-zebul; god of dung. <div eID="gen31403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31404" type="x-p"/> It is likely that it was Adonis who is called The dead, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.27">Lev 19:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.28">Lev 19:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.14.9">Deu 14:9</reference>, because he was worshipped as one dead. And the women represented as worshipping him were probably adulteresses, and had suffered through the jealousy of their husbands. And this worship of the image of jealousy provoked God to jealousy, to destroy this bad people.
entries.ca38caca38c896806ced4fc4be4218d9e7bf9d4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31405" type="x-p"/> The vision that I saw in the plain - see the note on <reference osisRef="Eze.3.23">Eze 3:23</reference> (note); see also <reference osisRef="Eze.1.3">Eze 1:3</reference> (note).
entries.95ca4fe01a264ebc7f71e5017b11ef6c18c3dd92: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen31405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31406" type="x-p"/> A hole in the wall - This we find was not large enough to see what was doing within; and the prophet is directed to dig, and make it larger, <reference osisRef="Eze.8.8">Eze 8:8</reference>; and when he had done so and entered, he says: -
entries.f405c94d04224f2824aeeda2134f109ce3f52444: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31407" type="x-p"/> And saw - every form of creeping things - It is very likely that these images pourtrayed on the wall were the objects of Egyptian adoration: the ox, the ape, the dog, the crocodile, the ibis, the scarabaeus or beetle, and various other things. It appears that these were privately worshipped by the sanhedrin or great Jewish council, consisting of seventy or seventy-two persons, six chosen out of every tribe, as representatives of the people. The images were pourtrayed upon the wall, as we find those ancient idols are on the walls of the tombs of the kings and nobles of Egypt. See the plates to Belzoni's Travels, the Isaic Tomb in the Bodleian Library, and the Egyptian hieroglyphics in general. Virgil speaks of these, Aen. lib. viii.: - <div eID="gen31407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31408" type="x-p"/> Omnigenumque Deum monstra, et latrator Anubis. "All kinds of gods, monsters, and barking dogs."
entries.64bba145350ba398d81499181e5766e3dd4b48d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen31408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31409" type="x-p"/> Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan - Shaphan was a scribe, or what some call comptroller of the temple, in the days of Josiah; and Jaazaniah his son probably succeeded him in this office. He was at the head of this band of idolaters.
entries.563440c6d8bf9cfbaac1e9492361dec1193c8e3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen31409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31410" type="x-p"/> There sat women weeping for Tammuz - This was Adonis, as we have already seen; and so the Vulgate here translates. My old MS. Bible reads, There saten women, mornynge a mawmete of lecherye that is cleped Adonrdes. He is fabled to have been a beautiful youth beloved by Venus, and killed by a wild boar in Mount Lebanon, whence springs the river Adonis, which was fabled to run blood at his festival in August. The women of Phoenicia, Assyria, and Judea worshipped him as dead, with deep lamentation, wearing priapi and other obscene images all the while, and they prostituted themselves in honor of this idol. Having for some time mourned him as dead, they then supposed him revivified and broke out into the most extravagant rejoicings. Of the appearance of the river at this season, Mr. Maundrell thus speaks: "We had the good fortune to see what is the foundation of the opinion which Lucian relates, viz., that this stream at certain seasons of the year, especially about the feast of Adonis, is of a bloody color, proceeding from a kind of sympathy, as the heathens imagined, for the death of Adonis, who was killed by a wild boar in the mountain out of which this stream issues. Something like this we saw actually come to pass, for the water was stained to a surprising redness; and, as we observed in travelling, had stained the sea a great way into a reddish hue." This was no doubt occasioned by a red ochre, over which the river ran with violence at this time of its increase. Milton works all this up in these fine lines: - "Thammuz came next behind, <div eID="gen31410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31411" type="x-p"/> Whose annual wound in Lebanon allured <div eID="gen31411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31412" type="x-p"/> The Syrian damsels to lament his fate, <div eID="gen31412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31413" type="x-p"/> In amorous ditties all a summer's day; <div eID="gen31413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31414" type="x-p"/> While smooth Adonis, from his native rock, <div eID="gen31414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31415" type="x-p"/> Ran purple to the sea, suffused with blood <div eID="gen31415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31416" type="x-p"/> Of Thammuz, yearly wounded. The love tale <div eID="gen31416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31417" type="x-p"/> Infected Sion's daughters with like heat: <div eID="gen31417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31418" type="x-p"/> Whose wanton passions in the sacred porch <div eID="gen31418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31419" type="x-p"/> Ezekiel saw, when by the vision led, <div eID="gen31419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31420" type="x-p"/> His eye surveyed the dark idolatries <div eID="gen31420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31421" type="x-p"/> Of alienated Judah." <div eID="gen31421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31422" type="x-p"/> Par. Lost, b. 1:446. <div eID="gen31422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31423" type="x-p"/> Tammuz signifies hidden or obscure, and hence the worship of his image was in some secret place.
entries.0676b5ee80f9a0a178e4b67db5e0868e133348e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen31423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31424" type="x-p"/> Five and twenty men - These most probably represented the twenty-four courses of the priests, with the high priest for the twenty-fifth. This was the Persian worship, as their turning their faces to the east plainly shows they were worshipping the rising sun.
entries.c305d076897bcf1bea2be5378eb2e2d17e9f62d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen31424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31425" type="x-p"/> They put the branch to their nose - This is supposed to mean some branch or branches, which they carried in succession in honor of the idol, and with which they covered their faces, or from which they inhaled a pleasant smell, the branches being odoriferous. That the heathens carried branches of trees in their sacred ceremonies is well known to all persons acquainted with classic antiquity; and it is probable that the heathen borrowed those from the use of such branches in the Jewish feast of tabernacles. There are many strange, and some filthy, interpretations given of this clause; but the former are not worth repeating, and I abominate the latter too much to submit to defile my paper with them. Probably the Brahminic Linga is here intended. <div eID="gen31425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31426" type="x-p"/> It really seems that at this time the Jews had incorporated every species of idolatry in their impure worship, - Phoenician, Egyptian, and Persian. I might add that some imagine the image of jealousy to be a personification of idolatry itself.  <chapter eID="Ezek.8"/> <div eID="gen31426" type="x-p"/>

entries.6fbbadcdb333b662959e2ba03dc325cc2de416a4: <div eID="gen14838" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Vision of the Destruction of Jerusalem - Ezekiel 8-11</title> <div sID="gen14839" type="x-p"/> A year and two months after his call, the glory of the Lord appeared to the prophet a second time, as he had seen it by the Chebar. He is transported in spirit to Jerusalem into the court of the temple (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1-Ezek.8.4">Eze 8:1-4</reference>), where the Lord causes him to see, first the idolatry of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.5-Ezek.8.18">Eze 8:5-18</reference>), and secondly, the judgment why, on account of this idolatry, all the inhabitants of Jerusalem are smitten (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.1-Ezek.9.11">Eze 9:1-11</reference>), the city is burned with fire, and the sanctuary forsaken by God (Ezekiel 10). Lastly, after he has been charged to foretell to the representatives of the people more especially the coming judgment, and to those who are sent into exile a future salvation (Ezekiel 11:1-21), he describes how the gracious presence of God forsakes the city before his own eyes (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.22-Ezek.11.23">Eze 11:22-23</reference>). After this has taken place, Ezekiel is carried back in the vision to Chaldea once more; and there, after the vision has come to an end, he announces to the exiles what he has seen and heard (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.24-Ezek.11.25">Eze 11:24-25</reference>). <div eID="gen14839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14840" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1-Ezek.8.4">Eze 8:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen14840" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Abominations of the Idolatry of the House of Israel</title> <div sID="gen14841" type="x-p"/> Time and place of the divine revelation. - Eze 8:1. <hi type="italic">And it came to pass in the sixth year, in the sixth (month), on the fifth (day) of the month, I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting before me; there fell upon me the hand of the Lord Jehovah there.</hi> Eze 8:2. <hi type="italic">And I saw, and behold a figure like the look of fire, from the look of its loins downwards fire, and from its loins upwards like a look of brilliance, like the sight of red-hot brass.</hi> Eze 8:3. <hi type="italic">And he stretched out the form of a hand, and took me by the locks of my head, and wind carried me away between earth and heaven, and brought me to Jerusalem in visions of God, to the entrance of the gate of the inner court, which faces towards the north, where the image of jealousy exciting jealousy had its stand.</hi> Eze 8:4. <hi type="italic">And, behold, the glory of the God of Israel was there, like the vision which I have seen in the valley.</hi> - The place where Ezekiel received this new theophany agrees with the statements in <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.24">Eze 3:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.4">Eze 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.6">Eze 4:6</reference>, that he was to shut himself up in his house, and lie 390 days upon the left side, and 40 days upon the right side - in all, 430 days. The use of the word יושׁב, “I sat,” is not at variance with this, as ישׁב does not of necessity signify sitting as contrasted with lying, but may also be used in the more general sense of staying, or living, in the house. Nor is the presence of the elders of Judah opposed to the command, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.24">Eze 3:24</reference>, to shut himself up in the house, as we have already observed in the notes on that passage. The new revelation is made to him in the presence of these elders, because it is of the greatest importance to them. They are to be witnesses of his ecstasy; and after this has left the prophet, are to hear from his lips the substance of the divine revelation (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.25">Eze 11:25</reference>). It is otherwise with the time of the revelation. If we compare the date given in <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1">Eze 8:1</reference> with those mentioned before, this new vision apparently falls within the period required for carrying out the symbolical actions of the previous vision. Between <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.1-Ezek.1.2">Eze 1:1-2</reference> (the fifth day of the fourth month in the fifth year) and <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1">Eze 8:1</reference> (the fifth day of the sixth month in the sixth year) we have one year and two months, that is to say (reckoning the year as a lunar year at 354 days, and the two months at 59 days), 413 days; whereas the two events recorded in Ezekiel 1-7 require at least 437 days, namely 7 days for <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.15">Eze 3:15</reference>, and 390 + 40 = 430 days for <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.5">Eze 4:5</reference>-6. Consequently the new theophany would fall within the 40 days, during which Ezekiel was to lie upon the right side for Judah. To get rid of this difficulty, Hitzig conjectures that the fifth year of Jehoiachin (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.2">Eze 1:2</reference>) was a leap year of 13 months or 385 days, by which he obtains an interval of 444 days after adding 59 for the two months, - a period sufficient not only to include the 7 days (<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.15">Eze 3:15</reference>) and 390 + 40 days (<reference osisRef="Ezek.4.5-Ezek.4.6">Eze 4:5-6</reference>), but to leave 7 days for the time that elapsed between Ezekiel 7 and 8. But however attractive this reckoning may appear, the assumption that the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin was a leap year is purely conjectural; and there is nothing whatever to give it probability. Consequently the only thing that could lead us to adopt such a solution, would be the impossibility of reconciling the conclusion to be drawn from the chronological data, as to the time of the two theophanies, with the substance of these divine revelations. <div eID="gen14841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14842" type="x-p"/> If we assume that Ezekiel carried out the symbolical acts mentioned in Ezekiel 4 and 5 in all their entirety, we can hardly imagine that the vision described in the chapters before us, by which he was transported in spirit to Jerusalem, occurred within the period of forty days, during which he was to typify the siege of Jerusalem by lying upon his right side. Nevertheless, Kliefoth has decided in favour of this view, and argues in support of it, that the vision described in Eze 8:1. took place in the prophet’s own house, that it is identical in substance with what is contained in Ezekiel 3:22-7:27, and that there is no discrepancy, because all that occurred here was purely internal, and the prophet himself was to address the words contained in <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.4-Ezek.11.12">Eze 11:4-12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.14-Ezek.11.21">Eze 11:14-21</reference> to the inhabitants of Jerusalem in his state of ecstasy. Moreover, when it is stated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.25">Eze 11:25</reference> that Ezekiel related to the exiles all that he had seen in the vision, it is perfectly open to us to assume that this took place at the same time as his report to them of the words of God in <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.1-Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:1-14</reference> and 7, and those which follow in Ezekiel 12. But. on the other hand, it may be replied that the impression produced by <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.25">Eze 11:25</reference> is not that the prophet waited several weeks after his visionary transport to Jerusalem before communicating to the elders what he saw in the vision. And even if the possibility of this cannot be disputed, we cannot imagine any reason why the vision should be shown to the prophet four weeks before it was to be related to the exiles. Again, there is not sufficient identity between the substance of the vision in Ezekiel 8-11 and the revelation in Ezekiel 4-7, to suggest any motive for the two to coincide. It is true that the burning of Jerusalem, which Ezekiel sees in Ezekiel 8-11, is consequent upon the siege and conquest of that city, which he has already predicted in Ezekiel 4-7 both in figure and word; but they are not so closely connected, that it was necessary on account of this connection for it to be shown to him before the completion of the symbolical siege of Jerusalem.
